extracted.intended_audience: startup founders and PR professionals seeking TechCrunch coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Practical step-by-step guidance for founders or PRs on preparing and pitching news to TechCrunch, including what to pitch, how to build relationships with reporters, embargo/exclusive strategy, and follow-up best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch topic selection / what to pitch (and what to skip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you pitch, you need to know which types of news and publication formats they care about. First, don't bother pitching ideas like partnerships, speaking events or team announcements (unless you’re Pinterest or GitHub).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, focus on things like raising investments or value-adding insights like pitch deck teardowns. TechCrunch is particularly interested in investment news. Features with interesting angles or expert op-eds from founders are also high on the list of pitches a journalist wants to receive. Examples: FlyFeed, Food Rocket and Quantori received coverage for investment rounds; We Do Solar was covered as a response to the European energy crisis; Seamm’s founder wrote an op-ed on M&A. Anti-pattern: pitching internal product tweaks or minor business announcements that don't change how people live or affect the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the publication (read the site & editorial guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can't make a successful pitch if you aren't familiar with the media. Spend time perusing the site, and don't try to pitch anything until you can perfectly describe their audience, topics they cover, which companies and experts regularly contribute and which topics are most in-demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find their editorial guidelines and discern whether they have specific startup coverage requirements. TechCrunch covers apps, consumer tech, fintech, greentech, hardware, media and entertainment, security, startups, transportation and venture. Practical: be able to describe audience and topic fit before pitching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build relationships with relevant journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the time to build a relationship with a relevant journalist. This is the step that most companies gloss over because it's time-consuming. However, it's a foundational part of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and follow journalists who might be interested in your news on Twitter. Interact with them and get to know which topics are of professional interest. Journalists get hundreds of pitches weekly; if you're just some random person your message may be ignored. For TechCrunch, reporters are divided by geography as well as topic — visit the staff page to ensure you connect with the right person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-check that your idea is newsworthy. One of the most frequent mistakes is thinking a product breakthrough or minor business announcement is important enough when it’s really not newsworthy at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness criteria: it must alter how people live their lives, impact the market or its competitive landscape, or cause readers to become invested in what will happen next. Practical anti-pattern: internal improvements or features that don't change user behavior are unlikely to be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose embargo vs exclusive strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: When offering news to an outlet, you need to decide whether it's under embargo or an exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embargoes: more common in the U.S. market; can be agreed with multiple outlets; benefits include coordinating newsflow across timezones, determining optimal coverage, and limiting inaccuracies by giving journalists time to prepare higher-quality material. Exclusives: offer the story to a single outlet only; give the potential for maximum efficiency and coverage if you choose the right reporter and the topic is noteworthy enough. Use exclusives for announcements like big collaborations with famous partners, impressive investments from well-known funds, or truly revolutionary product launches. Practical note: sending a mass email does not guarantee publication; an exclusive can be strategically better if matched to the right reporter and news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a brief, compelling pitch email
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists get mountains of pitches every day, so be respectful of their time and get straight to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distill your pitch to no more than seven sentences, and include company data, competitors, your brand's connection with the market and how your idea is relevant to current trends. Be concise and immediately signal why the story matters to the outlet's readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up etiquette and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Should you follow up? Absolutely. However, do so carefully and respectfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-ups should be well-timed and relevant. Don't bombard journalists — repeated, aggressive follow-ups can get you blacklisted. Example caution: the author once sent at least 30 follow-ups over nearly three months to secure coverage for a relatively small round; that persistence worked in that case but is not recommended for new contacts. Choose and stick to a follow-up strategy that balances persistence with respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review your pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Always check your pitch with peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outside eyes can give perspective and help refine talking points further. This is a quick sanity check to ensure clarity and newsworthiness before outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow sufficient lead time
rubrics_metrics.description: Give yourself at least three weeks of lead time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three weeks ensures a smooth pitch process and leaves breathing room for a backup plan if needed — useful when coordinating embargoes, journalist schedules, or extra reporting time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research individual journalists' preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Google tips for your specific journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journalists will post their preferences and suggestions online; taking time to look can improve targeting and pitch format. Tailor outreach based on publicly stated preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to access paywalled content
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest in the Extra Crunch subscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much of TechCrunch's content is behind a paywall; subscribing can give you full context for the outlet's coverage and help you craft a better-aligned pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consume news frequently to stay relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend at least an hour every day reading the latest news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daily news consumption helps you know what's relevant and interesting to journalists and spot timely hooks for your pitch.
